DNS.why_seen: Resolves domain names to IP addresses. Nearly every internet action starts with a DNS query.
DNS.who_uses: Every device on the network doing normal browsing, app usage, or system updates
DNS.who_exploits: Attackers performing DNS tunneling for data exfiltration, or DNS spoofing to redirect traffic
DNS.risk: Individually low risk, but DNS tunneling can smuggle data past firewalls disguised as normal queries
red_flags: Unusually long domain names (40+ characters) — possible DNS tunneling
High frequency of queries to a single unfamiliar domain
Queries to known malicious domains or DGA-pattern domains
DNS.real_world_example: APT groups have used DNS tunneling (e.g., DNSMessenger) to exfiltrate data while evading traditional firewall detection

TLS.why_seen: Encrypted communication — the foundation of HTTPS. Browsers, apps, and OS services all use it constantly.
TLS.who_uses: Any application making a secure connection — web browsers, cloud sync, messaging apps
TLS.who_exploits: Attackers cannot read TLS content directly, but weak/outdated TLS versions can be downgraded or exploited
TLS.risk: TLS 1.0/1.1 or weak cipher suites can be vulnerable to downgrade attacks like POODLE or BEAST
red_flags: TLS handshake using version 1.0 or 1.1 instead of 1.2/1.3
Self-signed or expired certificates in the handshake
Unusually large volume of TLS traffic to an unfamiliar IP
TLS.real_world_example: CVE-2014-3566 — POODLE attack exploiting SSLv3 fallback to decrypt secure communications

TCP.why_seen: Foundation of most internet communication — establishes reliable, ordered connections
TCP.who_uses: Nearly all application-layer protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, FTP) run on top of TCP
TCP.who_exploits: Attackers performing port scans, SYN floods, or connection hijacking
TCP.risk: A high volume of SYN packets without completed handshakes can indicate a port scan or SYN flood attack
red_flags: Many SYN packets to sequential ports from the same source — port scanning behavior
Repeated connection resets (RST) — possible firewall evasion attempt
Half-open connections in large volume — potential SYN flood
TCP.real_world_example: SYN flood attacks (a classic DoS technique) exploit TCP's three-way handshake by never completing it, exhausting server resources

HTTP.why_seen: Unencrypted web traffic — legacy or misconfigured web services still using plain HTTP
HTTP.who_uses: Older websites, internal tools, IoT devices, or misconfigured servers that haven't enabled HTTPS
HTTP.who_exploits: Attackers performing man-in-the-middle attacks to read or inject content into unencrypted traffic
HTTP.risk: All data — including credentials if submitted via forms — is visible in plaintext to anyone on the network path
red_flags: Login forms or credential submission over HTTP instead of HTTPS
Sensitive data (session cookies, tokens) visible in plaintext headers
Unexpected HTTP traffic to unfamiliar external IPs
HTTP.real_world_example: Firesheep (2010) demonstrated trivial session hijacking over public WiFi by sniffing unencrypted HTTP cookies

TELNET.why_seen: Legacy remote login protocol — should not appear on any modern, properly secured network
TELNET.who_uses: Outdated network equipment, legacy embedded systems, misconfigured devices
TELNET.who_exploits: Attackers sniffing the network can read usernames and passwords directly — no decryption needed
TELNET.risk: Complete credential exposure in plaintext — anyone capturing this traffic sees the password immediately
red_flags: Any Telnet traffic at all on a modern network is itself the red flag
Login prompts or credential strings visible directly in packet payload
TELNET.real_world_example: The Mirai botnet (2016) primarily spread by scanning the internet for devices with open Telnet and default credentials

FTP.why_seen: Unencrypted file transfer — legacy protocol still used by some web hosting and internal tools
FTP.who_uses: Legacy systems, some web developers still uploading via FTP instead of SFTP
FTP.who_exploits: Attackers sniffing credentials and file contents transmitted in plaintext
FTP.risk: Username, password, and all transferred file contents are visible to anyone capturing the traffic
red_flags: USER/PASS commands visible in plaintext in the packet payload
Large file transfers over FTP instead of encrypted alternatives
FTP.real_world_example: CVE-2011-2523 — vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor, widely exploited due to FTP's continued use on internet-facing servers

UDP.why_seen: Connectionless protocol used for speed-priority traffic — DNS, streaming, gaming, VoIP
UDP.who_uses: DNS queries, video streaming, online gaming, VoIP calls
UDP.who_exploits: Attackers using UDP for amplification DDoS attacks (DNS, NTP, memcached amplification)
UDP.risk: No handshake means source IPs are easily spoofed — heavily abused in reflection/amplification DDoS attacks
red_flags: Large volume of small UDP packets to a single destination — possible amplification attack source
UDP traffic on unusual high ports with no clear application
UDP.real_world_example: The 2018 GitHub DDoS attack used memcached UDP amplification to generate 1.35 Tbps of traffic

ICMP.why_seen: Network diagnostic protocol — used by ping, traceroute, and error reporting between devices
ICMP.who_uses: Network administrators troubleshooting connectivity; operating systems reporting network errors
ICMP.who_exploits: Attackers using ICMP tunneling to exfiltrate data, or ICMP flood for denial-of-service
ICMP.risk: ICMP tunneling can smuggle data past firewalls that don't inspect ICMP payload content
red_flags: Unusually large ICMP packet payloads — standard ping packets are small
High-frequency ICMP traffic — possible ICMP flood (Ping of Death variant)
ICMP traffic carrying non-standard payload patterns
ICMP.real_world_example: Loki ICMP tunneling tool has been used historically to covertly exfiltrate data through firewalls that permit ICMP

NTP.why_seen: Synchronizes your system clock with time servers. Almost every device does this automatically in the background.
NTP.who_uses: Operating systems and applications keeping accurate time — routers, laptops, phones, servers
NTP.who_exploits: Attackers using NTP servers for amplification DDoS attacks — small request, massive response sent to a spoofed victim
NTP.risk: Individually harmless, but misconfigured open NTP servers are heavily abused as DDoS amplification vectors
red_flags: NTP responses far larger than requests — classic amplification pattern
Same device sending MONLIST-style queries to many external NTP servers
NTP.real_world_example: 2014 saw record-breaking NTP amplification DDoS attacks exceeding 400 Gbps, exploiting the monlist command in older NTP implementations

ARP.why_seen: Maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local network. No IP layer involved — this is why source/destination show as N/A, ARP operates below IP.
ARP.who_uses: Every device on a local network, constantly, to know which physical device owns which IP
ARP.who_exploits: Attackers performing ARP spoofing/poisoning to redirect traffic through their own machine — classic man-in-the-middle setup
ARP.risk: ARP has no authentication built in — any device can claim to own any IP on the local segment, enabling traffic interception
red_flags: Duplicate or conflicting ARP replies for the same IP from different MAC addresses
Unusually high volume of ARP requests/replies — possible ARP flood or spoofing attempt
Gateway MAC address changing unexpectedly
ARP.real_world_example: ARP spoofing is the foundation of tools like Ettercap and Bettercap, used to intercept traffic on local networks via man-in-the-middle attacks
